sentences.text:
It is submitted on behalf of the petitioner that earlier this case was booked under Section 354 IPC,
read with Section 8 of the POCSO Act, on the basis of an FIR lodged on 18.05.2023.
The victim's statement was recorded under Section 161 CrPC on the same day and she was forwarded for medical examination on the same day.

After hearing about the incident, the father of the victim lodged the FIR and at that time, Section 376 (3) IPC, read with Section 6 of the POCSO Act was not incorporated, but on a later date, Section 376 (3) IPC and Section 6 of the POCSO Act was incorporated along with Section 354 IPC, read with Section 8 of the POCSO Act.
5. It is submitted that the victim may have been tutored.

The learned counsel for the petitioner has relied on the decision of Hon'ble the Supreme Court in Radhey Shyam - Vs- State of Rajasthan;
(2014) 5 SCC 389, wherein it was observed that- "12.

entities.text:
Radhey Shyam - Vs- State of Rajasthan;
(2014) 5 SCC 389
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In Panchhi, after reiterating the same principles, this Court observed that the evidence of a child witness must be evaluated more carefully and with greater circumspection because a child is susceptible to be swayed by what others tell him and, thus, a child witness is an easy prey to tutoring.
This Court further observed that the courts have held that the evidence of a child witness must find adequate corroboration before it is relied upon.
But, it is more a rule of practical wisdom than of law.
It is not necessary to refer to other judgments cited by learned counsel because they reiterate the same principles.
The conclusion which can be deduced from the relevant pronouncements of this Court is that the evidence of a child witness must be subjected to close scrutiny to rule out the possibility of tutoring.
It can be relied upon if the court finds that the child witness has sufficient intelligence and understanding of the obligation of an oath.
As a matter of caution, the court must find adequate corroboration to the child witness's evidence.
If found, reliable and truthful and corroborated by other evidence on record, it can be accepted without hesitation.
We will scrutinize PW-2 Banwari's evidence in Page No.# 3/5 light of the above principles."

6. Learned counsel for the petitioner has also relied on the decision of Hon'ble the Supreme Court in Amar Singh -Vs- State of Punjab; (1987) 1 SCC 679, wherein it was observed that- "10. xxxx xxxx xxxx xxxx Thus the evidence of P.W. 5. is totally inconsistent with the medical evidence.

sentences.text: It is trite that this Court does not, normally, interfere with an order passed by the High Court granting or rejecting bail to the accused.

However, it is equally incumbent upon the High Court to exercise its discretion judiciously, cautiously and strictly in compliance with the basic principles laid down in a plethora of decisions of this Court on the point.

The learned counsel for the informant and the learned Additional Public Prosecutor has also relied on the decision of the Hon'ble the Supreme Court in Kalyan Chandra Sarkar -Vs- Rajes Ranjan Alias Pappu Yadav & Another; (2004) 7 SCC 528, wherein it was observed that- "The law in regard to grant or refusal of bail is very well settled.

entities.text: Kalyan Chandra Sarkar -Vs- Rajes Ranjan Alias Pappu Yadav & Another; (2004) 7 SCC 528
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The Court granting bail should exercise its discretion in a judicious manner and not as a matter of course.

Though at the stage of granting bail a detailed examination of evidence and elaborate documentation of the merit of the case need not be undertaken, there is a need to indicate in such orders reasons for prima facie concluding why bail was being granted particularly where the accused is charged of having committed a serious offence.
Any order devoid of such reasons would suffer from non-application of mind.

sentences.text: 9. I have considered the submissions at the Bar with circumspection and I have also perused the Case Diary.
10. It is true that the petitioner is behind bars for 171 days.
11. Charges have been framed against the petitioner in the relevant case.

The evidence Page No.#
5/5 of the victim is yet to be recorded.
The victim may feel threatened to depose in the Court if the petitioner is enlarged on bail.
The petitioner occupies a formidable post in the school and most of the witnesses are students of the school.
At this juncture, the petitioner is not enlarged on bail.
Meanwhile, the learned trial Court is directed to expedite the trial and immediately record the statement of the victim.

12. The petition is rejected at this stage, with a liberty to the petitioner to approach the learned trial Court for bail after the evidence of the victim is recorded and the petition may be considered as per merits of the case.
